claims.text: The initial Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy is in a high-temperature BCC phase.
Cooling from the high-temperature BCC state first produces a transient short-range-ordered state.
The transient short-range order may be B2-type.
The transient ordered state temporarily stabilizes the alloy by minimizing its local free energy.
Subsequent thermal exposure activates diffusion that overprints the transient ordered state.
Thermally activated diffusion drives elemental segregation.
Diffusion-driven elemental segregation nucleates secondary phases such as FCC phases or intermetallic compounds.
Rapid quenching favors local atomic ordering and retention of a metastable ordered BCC or related structure.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit limited secondary-phase formation relative to more slowly cooled or thermally held samples.
Slower cooling or longer thermal holds will increase secondary-phase nucleation by enhancing atomic diffusion.
Competition between rapid ordering and slower diffusion governs the observed phase evolution.
The proposed mechanism should not operate at temperatures sufficiently low that diffusion is negligible.
Near-equilibrium high-temperature conditions may prevent the transient ordered state from being distinctly observable.
The cooling-rate and hold-time thresholds separating metastable ordering from diffusion-driven phase separation are not yet quantified.
